decisions.reason: A explicitly addresses B as 'Mr Edgar' in turn 1, directly establishing B's name/title.
'How's business?' in turn 1 presupposes that B has a business; this is a necessary existential presupposition of the question.
'Still booming' in turn 1 presupposes that the business was previously booming; 'still' requires a prior state of being booming to make sense.

decisions.claim: B is a customer of A's organization
decisions.reason: 'What can we do for you today?' is a generic service greeting that does not necessarily presuppose B is already a customer; B could be a first-time visitor or prospective customer. Turn 3's 'assign you a customer manager' suggests B may not yet have one, further weakening the claim that B is already a customer.
decisions.counterexample: B is a first-time visitor or prospective customer who has not yet been assigned a customer manager.

decisions.reason: c5 ('B is addressed as Mr Edgar') and c1 ('B's name is Mr Edgar') refer to the same evidential fact from the same quote in turn 1; c1 is the more informative canonical statement.

decisions.claim: B is a customer or prospective customer of A's company
decisions.reason: 'Assign you a customer manager' in turn 3 presupposes B is a customer or prospective customer of A's organization; the concept of a 'customer manager' implies a customer relationship exists or is being established.

decisions.claim: B currently deals with multiple people at A's company
decisions.reason: 'You don't need to deal with anyone else' is part of a proposal about what A's organization can do going forward; it does not necessarily presuppose that B currently deals with multiple people. A could be offering this as a simplification for someone who has only dealt with one person so far, or as a general policy statement.
decisions.counterexample: B has only dealt with one person so far, and A is offering a single point of contact as a convenience or policy.
